decouverte.titre: Four problems in the same week
paragraphes: This week, your school had four problems. A student copied homework from the internet. Some computers were stolen.
A family asked for money for a broken phone. An inspector came to check if the canteen was clean.
Nobody solved these problems in the same way. An investigation means looking for facts to learn what happened. In security, there are four kinds of investigations.

decouverte.comme: For the copied homework, the principal looks into it alone. For the stolen computers, the police come. For the broken phone, a judge decides between two families. For the canteen, a government inspector checks a rule.
decouverte.enVrai: The four types are called administrative, criminal, civil and regulatory. Each one has its own investigator, its own level of proof and its own results. You will learn them one by one. The image is simple: real cases are more complex.

decouverte.question: An employee downloads movies with the company internet, against the rules. Who MOST likely investigates?
options: The police
The company itself
A court
decouverte.explanation: This breaks a company rule. Nobody outside is hurt. So the company looks into it alone. This is an administrative investigation.

decouverte.texte: A company learns that a former worker copied customer files. It can look into the case inside the company. It can call the police. It can go to court to ask for money. And a government office can check how the data was protected.

decouverte.titre: The rules change from country to country
decouverte.comme: School rules change from one school to another. What is allowed at your school may be banned in another school.
decouverte.enVrai: Laws and courts also change from country to country. The manual uses English common law as an example. This is law built on past court decisions. You must learn the rules of your own country and of your clients.

cards.question: A company looks into a worker who broke its rules. Only the company takes part. There is no police and no court. Which type of investigation is this?
options: A criminal investigation led by the police
An administrative investigation
A civil investigation in court
A regulatory investigation by an agency
options_why: The police lead criminal cases for the State. Here, no police take part.
Civil cases are disputes between two private parties. Here, nobody sues.
Regulatory cases check an official rule, and an agency leads them. Here, no agency takes part.
cards.answer: An administrative investigation
cards.explanation: The company looks into itself. This is what administrative means.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: A government agency checks if a restaurant follows the hygiene rules. Which type of investigation is this?
options: An administrative investigation inside the restaurant
A civil investigation between two companies
A criminal investigation of the owner
A regulatory investigation
options_why: The restaurant is not looking into itself. A government agency does the check.
Civil cases are disputes between private parties. Here, an agency checks a rule.
Criminal cases are about a crime. Here, the agency only checks if a rule is followed.
cards.answer: A regulatory investigation
cards.explanation: An agency checks if an official rule is followed. This is a regulatory investigation.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Two private companies argue about money in court. Which type of investigation supports this case?
options: A civil investigation
A criminal investigation led by the State
A regulatory investigation by an agency
An administrative investigation by one company
options_why: The State is not accusing anyone of a crime here.
No agency is checking an official rule here.
Administrative means one organization looking into itself. Here, two companies argue.
cards.answer: A civil investigation
cards.explanation: A dispute between two private parties is a civil case.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Police officers look into the theft of customer data by a hacker. The State wants to punish the hacker. Which type of investigation is this?
options: An administrative investigation
A civil investigation
A criminal investigation
A regulatory investigation
options_why: Administrative cases stay inside one organization. Here, the police and the State take part.
Civil cases are about money between private parties. Here, the State accuses a hacker.
Regulatory cases check an official rule. Here, the topic is a crime.
cards.answer: A criminal investigation
cards.explanation: The State prosecutes a person who broke the law. This is a criminal investigation.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: A former employee copied customer files. The company wants money for the harm. Which type of investigation fits BEST?
options: A criminal investigation
An administrative investigation
A civil investigation
A regulatory investigation
options_why: A criminal case is led by the State to punish a crime. The company wants money, not a punishment.
Administrative cases stay inside the company. Here, the company wants money from a former worker.
No agency is checking an official rule in this case.
cards.answer: A civil investigation
cards.explanation: When a private party asks for money for a loss, it is a civil case.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: What are the four types of investigations in the manual?
cards.answer: Administrative, criminal, civil and regulatory.
cards.explanation: Think of four investigators: the management, the police, a judge between two sides, and an inspector.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four types of investigations in the manual?
options: A commercial investigation
An administrative investigation
A regulatory investigation
A civil investigation
options_why: This is one of the four types in the manual.
This is one of the four types in the manual.
This is one of the four types in the manual.
cards.answer: A commercial investigation
cards.explanation: The four types are administrative, criminal, civil and regulatory. There is no commercial type.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Your company starts to work in a new country. A worker may need to run an investigation there. What should the security professional do FIRST?
options: Use the same steps as in the home country
Start to collect evidence at once
Ask the police to run the investigation
Learn the laws that apply in that place
options_why: Laws and courts change by country. The same steps may not work.
Collecting evidence with the rules of another place can make it useless.
The police do not run every investigation. The company must first know its own duties.
cards.answer: Learn the laws that apply in that place
cards.explanation: Laws and courts change a lot from one place to another. You must know the rules of your place and of your clients.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: What three things does the manual compare for each type of investigation?
cards.answer: Who does the investigation, how much proof is needed, and how the types are different.
cards.explanation: Think: who, how much proof, and what is different.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Which legal tradition does the manual use as an example to explain investigations?
options: French civil law
English common law
The law of the European Union
International law
options_why: The manual does not use French law as its base.
The manual does not use European law for this example.
The manual does not base the example on international law.
cards.answer: English common law
cards.explanation: The manual says this is only an example. Each country has its own rules.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. The manual says its information is largely based on English common law, strictly as an example.

cards.question: A company learns that a former worker stole customer data. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: Only a criminal investigation can follow
More than one type of investigation can follow
Only an administrative investigation can follow
The company must choose one type and cannot change it
options_why: A criminal case is possible, but the company can also sue for money.
The company can look into the case inside, but other types can follow.
Management can move from one type to another when it learns more.
cards.answer: More than one type of investigation can follow
cards.explanation: One case can lead to several investigations, one after another.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: What is evidence?
cards.answer: Something, like a document, a log or a file, that shows a fact is true.
cards.explanation: Without evidence, an investigation is only an opinion.
cards.explanation_more: Simple definition, outside the manual. A log is a record of what happened on a computer. The manual talks about evidence in this whole section.

cards.question: Which pair of investigation type and main investigator is correct?
options: Administrative: a government inspector
Civil: a regulatory agency
Regulatory: the company's own management
Criminal: law enforcement
options_why: An administrative investigation is led from inside the organization, not by an inspector.
A civil case is a dispute between private parties. An agency does not lead it.
A regulatory investigation is led by a government agency, not by the company.
cards.answer: Criminal: law enforcement
cards.explanation: Criminal cases are led by law enforcement, for the State.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: How can one case lead to more than one type of investigation?
cards.answer: Management can move from one type to another. For example, from administrative to civil or criminal.
cards.explanation: A company rule, a law and a dispute can all be involved in the same event.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Administrative”: management may escalate to civil actions or criminal charges.

cards.question: Which case is LEAST likely to be an administrative investigation?
options: Police look into a hacker who attacked a bank
Management checks who shared files against policy
Management looks into a worker who broke the internet rule
A company checks who leaked its plans, against its rules
options_why: This is an internal rule case. It stays inside the company.
This is an internal rule case. The company looks into itself.
This is an internal rule case. The company handles it alone.
cards.answer: Police look into a hacker who attacked a bank
cards.explanation: A hacker who attacks a bank is a case for the police. This is a criminal case.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Why must a security professional learn the laws of their own country?
cards.answer: Laws and courts change a lot around the world. The manual uses English common law only as an example.
cards.explanation: Using the rules of another country can make an investigation fail.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. It is essential to know the laws and rules of your place and of your customers.

paragraphes: Lucas says: “Emma took my notebook!” The teacher asks: “Do you have proof?”
Lucas has nothing: no witness and no trace. Emma is not punished. She does not have to prove that she is innocent.
The person who accuses must bring the proof. In court, this duty has a name: the burden of proof.

decouverte.titre: The teacher is like the judge
decouverte.comme: The teacher does not just listen to Lucas. She waits for solid facts. Until she gets them, Emma is treated as innocent.
decouverte.enVrai: The one who accuses must prove it. In a criminal case (the State accuses someone of a crime), this is the prosecutor. In a civil case (a dispute between two private parties), it is the plaintiff, who asks for money for a loss. The one who defends is the defendant. The image has limits: a teacher can follow a feeling, but a court needs solid proof.

decouverte.question: In a trial, who must bring the proof?
options: The one who accuses
The one who is accused
The judge
decouverte.explanation: That is the burden of proof: whoever accuses must show that the claim is true. The judge weighs the evidence. The accused has nothing to prove.

decouverte.texte: A company says that a former worker stole files. The company must prove it, for example with logs. A log is a record of who connected and when. The former worker does not have to show that he did nothing. Until the claim is proven, he is treated as innocent.

cards.question: Official definition: “burden of proof”
cards.answer: Burden of proof is the requirement that the criminal prosecutor or civil plaintiff/claimant prove the claims they are making against the accused, or defendant.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the person who accuses must prove it. Think of Lucas and the notebook.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”. A burden is a heavy load that you must carry.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “burden of proof”?
options: Burden of proof is the requirement that the accused, or defendant, prove that the claims made against them are false.
Burden of proof is the requirement that the judge prove the claims made by the criminal prosecutor or civil plaintiff/claimant.
Burden of proof is the requirement that the criminal prosecutor or civil plaintiff/claimant prove the claims they are making against the accused, or defendant.
Burden of proof is the requirement that the criminal prosecutor or civil plaintiff/claimant only suggest the claims they are making against the accused, or defendant.
options_why: This turns the rule around. The accused does not have to prove anything.
The judge weighs the evidence. The judge does not have to prove the claims.
Suggesting is not enough. The accuser must prove the claims with evidence.
cards.answer: Burden of proof is the requirement that the criminal prosecutor or civil plaintiff/claimant prove the claims they are making against the accused, or defendant.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: the criminal prosecutor or civil plaintiff, prove, and the accused, or defendant.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “burden of proof” from memory.
cards.answer: Burden of proof is the requirement that the criminal prosecutor or civil plaintiff/claimant prove the claims they are making against the accused, or defendant.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the accuser (prosecutor or plaintiff), the duty to prove, and the accused or defendant.

cards.question: Official definition: the one who accuses and the one who defends
cards.answer: The party making a claim must demonstrate the truth of that claim, with compelling evidence; the entity defending against the claim, in most modern societies, is presumed innocent or without fault — that is, the court will not recognize the validity of a claim against anyone until that claim is substantiated and the defendant is proven guilty.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the accuser must show that the claim is true. The other side is seen as innocent until then.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”. Compelling means very convincing. Substantiated means backed up with evidence.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about the one who accuses and the one who defends from memory.
cards.answer: The party making a claim must demonstrate the truth of that claim, with compelling evidence; the entity defending against the claim, in most modern societies, is presumed innocent or without fault — that is, the court will not recognize the validity of a claim against anyone until that claim is substantiated and the defendant is proven guilty.
cards.explanation: Three parts: compelling evidence, presumed innocent, and proven guilty.

cards.question: Official definition: the two standards of proof in the United States
cards.answer: In the U.S. legal system, the two predominant standards of proof that must be met are called preponderance of the evidence and beyond a reasonable doubt.
cards.explanation: In simple words: there are two levels of proof. The next planet explains both of them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about the two standards of proof from memory.
cards.answer: In the U.S. legal system, the two predominant standards of proof that must be met are called preponderance of the evidence and beyond a reasonable doubt.
cards.explanation: The number (two), then the two names in order.

cards.question: In a trial, who must bring the proof?
options: The person who is accused
The judge who hears the case
The person who makes the accusation
The first witness who speaks
options_why: The accused is presumed innocent and has nothing to prove.
The judge weighs the evidence. The judge does not search for proof for the accuser.
A witness can give facts, but the accuser must bring the proof.
cards.answer: The person who makes the accusation
cards.explanation: This is the burden of proof: whoever accuses must show that the claim is true.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: A company accuses an employee of a data leak. It has no log and no witness. What does the presumption of innocence say?
options: He is treated as innocent until the claim is proven
He must prove that he is innocent
The judge must look for the proof in place of the company
The company can punish him if it feels very sure about it
options_why: It is the opposite. The accuser must prove, not the accused.
The judge weighs the evidence. The judge does not take the accuser's place.
A feeling is not proof. The company must show evidence first.
cards.answer: He is treated as innocent until the claim is proven
cards.explanation: A court does not accept a claim until evidence backs it up.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Who makes the accusation in a criminal case?
options: The civil plaintiff, for a private party
The defendant, who defends himself
The judge, who decides the case
The criminal prosecutor, for the State
options_why: A civil plaintiff accuses in a civil case, not in a criminal case.
The defendant is the person who is accused.
The judge weighs the evidence. The judge does not accuse anyone.
cards.answer: The criminal prosecutor, for the State
cards.explanation: In a criminal case, the State accuses. The prosecutor speaks for the State.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Who makes the accusation in a criminal trial?
cards.answer: The criminal prosecutor, who speaks for the State.
cards.explanation: In a criminal case, it is the State that prosecutes.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Who carries the burden of proof in a civil case?
options: The defendant, who is sued by the plaintiff
The plaintiff (the claimant)
The criminal prosecutor, for the State
The judge, who hears the case
options_why: The defendant is the person who is sued. The defendant does not have to prove anything.
A criminal prosecutor works in criminal cases, not in civil cases.
The judge weighs the evidence but does not bring the proof.
cards.answer: The plaintiff (the claimant)
cards.explanation: In a civil case, a private party asks for money or relief. That party must prove the claim.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: A company wants to sue a former worker for taking files. It has only a feeling that he did it. What is the BEST advice?
options: Ask the former worker to show that he did not do it
Collect evidence first. The company must prove its claim
Start the case now and let the judge search for the proof
Wait until the former worker admits what he did
options_why: This turns the rule around. The accuser must prove the claim.
The judge weighs the evidence that the sides bring. The judge does not search for it.
Waiting for a confession is not a plan. The company can collect its own evidence.
cards.answer: Collect evidence first. The company must prove its claim
cards.explanation: The company is the accuser, so it carries the burden of proof. It needs evidence before it goes to court.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Which statement about the defendant is NOT correct?
options: The defendant is presumed innocent until the claim is proven
The defendant is the person who defends against the claim
The court does not accept a claim against him without evidence
The defendant must prove that he is innocent
options_why: This is correct. In most modern societies the defendant is presumed innocent.
This is correct. The defendant defends against the claim.
This is correct. A claim needs evidence before the court accepts it.
cards.answer: The defendant must prove that he is innocent
cards.explanation: The defendant never has to prove his innocence. The accuser must prove the claim.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Who makes the claim in a civil trial?
cards.answer: The civil plaintiff, also called the claimant.
cards.explanation: In a civil case, a private party asks for money for a loss.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Which person is MOST likely to carry the burden of proof?
options: A plaintiff who sues a company for a loss
A defendant who is sued by a private company
A judge who hears a civil case between two firms
An accused person in a criminal trial at court
options_why: The defendant answers the claim. The defendant does not carry the burden.
The judge weighs the evidence. The judge does not bring it.
The accused is presumed innocent. The prosecutor carries the burden.
cards.answer: A plaintiff who sues a company for a loss
cards.explanation: The person who makes the claim must prove it. In a civil case, this is the plaintiff.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: A court gets a claim against someone. What must happen FIRST before the court accepts the claim?
options: The accused must give his own version of events
The accused must admit that he did it
The claim must be backed up with evidence
A second court must agree with the claim
options_why: The accused can speak, but the accuser must still bring evidence.
A confession is not required. Evidence is what the court needs.
No second court is needed. One court decides on the evidence.
cards.answer: The claim must be backed up with evidence
cards.explanation: The court will not recognize a claim until it is backed up by evidence.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: What do we call the person who defends against the claim?
cards.answer: The accused, also called the defendant.
cards.explanation: This person is presumed innocent until the claim is proven.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: In most modern societies, why is a person presumed innocent at first?
options: Most accused people are innocent in real life
The accused person can pay for a lawyer
A court accepts a claim only when it is proven
Proving innocence is the job of the judge
options_why: This may be true or not. The rule does not depend on how many people are innocent.
Money has nothing to do with it. The rule protects everyone.
The judge weighs evidence. Nobody has to prove his innocence.
cards.answer: A court accepts a claim only when it is proven
cards.explanation: We do not punish someone on a simple word. The claim must be proven first.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Which party has the LEAST to prove in a trial?
options: The defendant
The civil plaintiff
The criminal prosecutor
The party that makes the claim
options_why: The plaintiff makes the claim, so the plaintiff must prove it.
The prosecutor makes the accusation, so the prosecutor must prove it.
The party that makes the claim carries the burden of proof.
cards.answer: The defendant
cards.explanation: The defendant is presumed innocent and does not have to prove anything.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: In your own words: what is the burden of proof? Give an example from school.
cards.answer: It is the duty of the accuser to prove the claim. Example: Lucas says Emma took his notebook, so Lucas must prove it.
cards.explanation: Whoever claims must show.

paragraphes: A teacher thinks Marie forgot her book. He gives her a small warning. He does not need to be 100 percent sure.
To send a student away for good, the school board must be much more sure. A mistake would cost too much.
The bigger the decision, the stronger the proof must be. In court, there are two levels of proof. They are called standards of proof.

decouverte.comme: Imagine a scale. For a small decision, it is enough if it tips a little to one side. For a very serious decision, it must tip so far that nobody can doubt.
decouverte.enVrai: In a civil case, it is enough that the scale tips a little. This is more likely than not (preponderance of the evidence). In a criminal case, it must tip so far that a reasonable person has no doubt. This is beyond a reasonable doubt. The image has limits: a judge does not use a real scale.

decouverte.question: Which of these two trials needs the stronger proof?
options: A civil trial between two companies
A criminal trial where prison is possible
decouverte.answer: A criminal trial where prison is possible
decouverte.explanation: When a person risks prison, we want to be almost sure before we convict. In a civil case, the stakes are mostly about money.

decouverte.texte: An employee is accused of stealing data. In a civil case, the company asks for money. It must show that it is more likely than not that he is responsible. In a criminal case, the State wants to convict him. It must prove his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

cards.question: Official definition: “preponderance of the evidence”
cards.answer: Preponderance of the evidence is the lower standard of the two and is used primarily in civil actions. It essentially means that the evidence shows that the defendant is more likely to have caused the damage than not.
cards.explanation: In simple words: it is the lower level of proof. The judge must think the defendant is more likely responsible than not.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”. A civil action is a trial between private parties.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “preponderance of the evidence”?
options: Preponderance of the evidence is the higher standard of the two and is used primarily in criminal actions. It essentially means that the evidence shows that the defendant is more likely to have caused the damage than not.

Preponderance of the evidence is the lower standard of the two and is used primarily in civil actions. It essentially means that the evidence shows that the defendant caused the damage with no doubt at all.
Preponderance of the evidence is the lower standard of the two and is used primarily in civil actions. It essentially means that the evidence shows that the defendant might have caused the damage.

Preponderance of the evidence is the lower standard of the two and is used primarily in civil actions. It essentially means that the evidence shows that the defendant is more likely to have caused the damage than not.
options_why: This swaps the two standards. The higher standard, used in criminal cases, is another one.
This is much too strong. It describes the higher standard, with no doubt at all.
Might have caused is too weak. The evidence must show more likely than not.
cards.answer: Preponderance of the evidence is the lower standard of the two and is used primarily in civil actions. It essentially means that the evidence shows that the defendant is more likely to have caused the damage than not.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: lower standard, civil actions, and more likely than not.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “preponderance of the evidence” from memory.
cards.answer: Preponderance of the evidence is the lower standard of the two and is used primarily in civil actions. It essentially means that the evidence shows that the defendant is more likely to have caused the damage than not.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the lower standard, used in civil actions, and more likely than not.

cards.question: Official definition: “beyond a reasonable doubt”
cards.answer: The second standard, beyond a reasonable doubt, is much harder to prove and is used primarily in criminal actions.
cards.explanation: In simple words: this is the high level of proof. It is much harder to reach. It is used in criminal cases.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”. A criminal action is a trial where the State prosecutes.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “beyond a reasonable doubt”?
options: The second standard, beyond a reasonable doubt, is much easier to prove and is used primarily in civil actions.
The second standard, beyond a reasonable doubt, is much harder to prove and is used primarily in criminal actions.
The second standard, beyond a reasonable doubt, is much harder to prove and is used primarily in civil actions.
The first standard, beyond a reasonable doubt, is slightly harder to prove and is used primarily in criminal actions.
options_why: This is the other way round. Beyond a reasonable doubt is hard to prove and used in criminal cases.
The level is right, but the field is different. This standard is mainly for criminal actions.
It is the second standard, and it is much harder to prove, not slightly harder.
cards.answer: The second standard, beyond a reasonable doubt, is much harder to prove and is used primarily in criminal actions.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: the second standard, much harder to prove, and criminal actions.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “beyond a reasonable doubt” from memory.
cards.answer: The second standard, beyond a reasonable doubt, is much harder to prove and is used primarily in criminal actions.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the second standard, much harder to prove, and criminal actions.

cards.question: Official definition: what “beyond a reasonable doubt” asks of the evidence
cards.answer: It is insufficient for the evidence to merely make the judge or jury lean more toward guilt than not. In this case, the evidence has to be so clear and compelling that a "reasonable" person has no doubt or reservation about the defendant's guilt after seeing it.
cards.explanation: In simple words: leaning toward guilt is not enough. A reasonable person must have no doubt left.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”.

cards.question: Say the official text about what “beyond a reasonable doubt” asks of the evidence from memory.
cards.answer: It is insufficient for the evidence to merely make the judge or jury lean more toward guilt than not. In this case, the evidence has to be so clear and compelling that a "reasonable" person has no doubt or reservation about the defendant's guilt after seeing it.
cards.explanation: Three parts: leaning is not enough, so clear and compelling, and no doubt or reservation.

cards.question: Official definition: the chance needed for the “preponderance of the evidence”
cards.answer: In other words, the evidence convinced the judge, jury, or ruling body that there was at least a 51 percent chance that the defendant caused the damage.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the judge must see a chance a little above 50 percent.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand Requirements for Investigation Types”. Later, the manual says 50.1 percent. Remember: a little more than half.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about the chance needed for the preponderance of the evidence from memory.
cards.answer: In other words, the evidence convinced the judge, jury, or ruling body that there was at least a 51 percent chance that the defendant caused the damage.
cards.explanation: Three parts: who is convinced, the 51 percent chance, and that the defendant caused the damage.

cards.question: In a civil trial, how sure must the court be that the defendant caused the damage?
options: It must be sure beyond a reasonable doubt
It is enough that it is more likely than not
