The manual names federal agencies.
The manual names international agencies.
cards.answer: Corporate agencies
cards.explanation: The manual names local, state, federal and international agencies. Companies are not law enforcement.

cards.question: Which techniques do criminal investigators use on computer evidence?
cards.answer: Investigation techniques, including digital forensics.
cards.explanation: Digital forensics means finding and studying evidence in digital devices.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Criminal”. Digital forensics is covered in domain 7.

cards.question: How does a criminal investigator work as the case grows? Which order is correct?
options: Precise laws first, then suspects and evidence, then the facts
Facts first, then suspects and evidence, then precise laws
Suspects first, then precise laws, then the facts of the case
The court first, then the facts, then suspects and evidence
options_why: The investigator cannot choose laws before knowing what happened.
Naming suspects before knowing the facts is risky.
A court is chosen only when the case is ready.
cards.answer: Facts first, then suspects and evidence, then precise laws
cards.explanation: The field narrows little by little: facts, then suspects and evidence, then specific laws.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a reason the manual gives for dropping or passing on a case?
options: Jurisdiction problems
The size of the victim company
The cost compared with the size of the crime
The chance of a successful prosecution
options_why: The manual names this reason.
The manual names this reason.
The manual names this reason.
cards.answer: The size of the victim company
cards.explanation: The manual names jurisdiction, cost against scale, and the chance of success. The size of the victim is not a reason.

cards.question: Why is a criminal case not only the company's business?
cards.answer: Because the State prosecutes people who break its laws.
cards.explanation: The company can ask for help, but the State leads the case.

concepts.name: The right moves when a crime is suspected

decouverte.titre: The first one on the scene
paragraphes: You are in charge of security at your company. One morning, you see that a stranger copied customer files during the night.
You want to search every computer to find who did it. It seems logical. But it is a bad idea.
Every click can erase traces. When you suspect a crime, your job is not to investigate alone.

decouverte.titre: The first witness of an accident
decouverte.comme: You are the first to see an accident. You call for help and you make the place safe. You do not move anything. The experts will find out what happened.
decouverte.enVrai: At work, it is the same. You limit the damage right away. This is called containment. You tell management and you let the authorities lead the investigation. The image has limits: you are not passive, you protect the systems at once.

decouverte.comme: A teacher keeps a notebook that shows who held the school key and when. If the key is lost, she can see who had it last.
decouverte.enVrai: The chain of custody is the same idea for evidence. It is a written record of who held the evidence and when. It shows that nobody changed it.

decouverte.question: You suspect a crime in your company. What is the best first action?
options: Search the computers to find the guilty person
Limit the damage and tell management
Call the police without telling anyone
decouverte.answer: Limit the damage and tell management
decouverte.explanation: Searching can damage the evidence. Calling alone is not your role: the decision is made with management and a lawyer.

decouverte.texte: To enter a company's computers, the police may need a court order. This is a paper from a court, such as a warrant or a subpoena (an order to hand over documents). But if the company calls the police itself, it can let them in. The company owns its computers.

cards.question: You suspect that a crime was committed in your company. Which action is the BEST first action?
options: Search all the computers to find the guilty person quickly
Call the police without telling anyone
Wait a week to see if it happens again
Limit the immediate damage and tell management
options_why: People without training can damage the evidence and get in the way of the investigation.
The decision to call the police is made with management and a lawyer.
Waiting lets the damage grow and puts the evidence at risk.
cards.answer: Limit the immediate damage and tell management
cards.explanation: You pass the information up right away, and you let the authorities decide what comes next.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Criminal”: suspend investigative activity, beyond containment of immediate damage, and escalate to management.

cards.question: Can a security professional decide alone to call the police about a suspected crime?
options: No, the decision is made with management and a lawyer
Yes, it is always the first duty of the security team
Yes, but only after a full personal investigation of the case
No, only the police can start a report
options_why: It is a complex decision. It does not belong to one single employee.
A personal investigation can damage the evidence.
Anyone can report a crime. The point is who decides for the company.
cards.answer: No, the decision is made with management and a lawyer
cards.explanation: The decision has effects on the whole company. Management and a lawyer (counsel) decide.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Criminal”. Counsel means a lawyer inside or outside the company.

cards.question: Why should an untrained employee not investigate a crime alone?
options: He may find the guilty person too fast
He will not be paid for the extra work
He can taint the evidence for the police
Only managers have the right to read files
options_why: Finding the person is not the problem. Damaging the evidence is.
Pay is not the reason for the rule.
Many workers read files for their job. The risk is to the evidence.
cards.answer: He can taint the evidence for the police
cards.explanation: Without training, he may change or destroy traces. We say the evidence becomes tainted.

cards.question: What can you keep doing after you suspect a crime?
cards.answer: Only limit the immediate damage (containment). Then tell management and wait for instructions.
cards.explanation: Limiting the damage is not investigating.

cards.question: A company asks the police for help and opens its own servers to them. Is a court order needed?
options: Yes, in every case, with no exception
Yes, unless the data is encrypted
No, the company owns them and can allow access
No, but only if the company is small
options_why: The owner of the property can give permission to anyone it wants.
Encryption is not the test. What counts is who owns the equipment.
The size of the company does not matter.
cards.answer: No, the company owns them and can allow access
cards.explanation: The owner can allow access to anyone it chooses, including the police.

cards.question: While you wait for the police, a colleague wants to copy the stranger's files himself, to save them. What is the BEST response?
options: Tell him to stop, because he could damage the evidence
Let him do it, because saving files is good
Let him do it if he has IT skills
Copy the files yourself to be safe
options_why: Even a good idea can change or erase traces.
Skill is not the problem. Only trained people should handle evidence.
You would put the same traces at risk.
cards.answer: Tell him to stop, because he could damage the evidence
cards.explanation: Untrained actions can taint the evidence. Leave the work to the right people.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a good action when you suspect a crime?
options: Warn management right away
Limit the immediate damage
Wait for instructions from the police or the authorities
Search the disks alone to find the guilty person
options_why: This is a good action. Management must know quickly.
This is a good action. Containment is allowed.
This is a good action. The authorities lead the investigation.
cards.answer: Search the disks alone to find the guilty person
cards.explanation: Searching alone can damage the evidence. Protect, warn and wait.

cards.question: Why should you not search the computers yourself?
cards.answer: Without training, you can damage the traces. This is called tainting the evidence.
cards.explanation: Damaged evidence may become unusable.

cards.question: Which people MOST likely have to follow strict rules such as warrants and chain of custody?
options: A company that chooses to give its own data to the police
Government investigators who work for law enforcement
A security manager who reports a crime
A private lawyer of the company
options_why: A company that owns evidence can choose to give it.
A manager who reports a crime does not run the investigation.
A company lawyer advises the company. Public investigators follow the strict rules.
cards.answer: Government investigators who work for law enforcement
cards.explanation: Law enforcement and prosecutors must follow strict rules for collecting and handling evidence.

cards.question: Which action has the LEAST risk of harming the evidence?
options: Searching the disks to see what changed
Limiting the damage and waiting for instructions
Deleting the suspicious files at once
Restarting every server to clear the problem
options_why: Searching can change dates and other traces.
Deleting removes the evidence itself.
Restarting can erase data that is only in memory.
cards.answer: Limiting the damage and waiting for instructions
cards.explanation: Containment protects the systems without changing the traces.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Criminal”. The detail about data in memory is outside the manual.

cards.question: Why is calling the police decided with management and a lawyer?
cards.answer: It is a complex decision with effects on the company. A lawyer knows the rules to follow.
cards.explanation: One person alone rarely sees all the risks.

cards.question: You limited the damage and told management. What is the BEST next step?
options: Start your own investigation of all the computers
Ask the staff who they think did it
Contact the media to find witnesses
Wait for guidance from management and a lawyer
options_why: Your own search can taint the evidence.
This can spread rumors and does not give reliable evidence.
The media can harm the case and the company.
cards.answer: Wait for guidance from management and a lawyer
cards.explanation: After containment, you suspend your own investigation and follow instructions.

cards.question: The police want data from a private company that refuses to help. What can give them the right to get it?
options: A court order, such as a warrant or a subpoena
A report from a security consultant
A letter from the company's insurer
A request from the victim's customers
options_why: A consultant report is not a legal order.
An insurer has no legal power over the company.
Customers cannot give the police this right.
cards.answer: A court order, such as a warrant or a subpoena
cards.explanation: A court order gives the State the right to get into private property, devices and data.

cards.question: What is a chain of custody?
cards.answer: The written record of who held the evidence, and when. It shows that nobody changed it.
cards.explanation: It is the logbook of where the evidence has been.
cards.explanation_more: Simple definition, outside the manual. The manual lists the chain of custody among the strict rules for public investigators.

cards.question: Who can issue a court order such as a warrant or a subpoena?
options: Only the head of the police
Any security manager
A judge, or sometimes an officer of the court
The victim company's lawyer
options_why: The police ask for orders. They do not issue them.
A manager has no such power.
A company lawyer can ask, but cannot issue a court order.
cards.answer: A judge, or sometimes an officer of the court
cards.explanation: Some orders must come from a judge. Others can come from an officer of the court, such as a prosecutor.

cards.question: Name two forms of a court order for getting evidence.
cards.answer: A warrant and a subpoena (an order to hand over documents).
cards.explanation: These orders give the State the right to get into private property, devices and data.

paragraphes: In the yard, Tom breaks Sacha's phone. Sacha's parents ask for money to fix it.
Nobody calls the police. Nobody goes to prison. It is a dispute between two families, and they want someone to repair the harm.
If the families do not agree, they go to a judge. This kind of dispute between private parties is called a civil case.

decouverte.comme: The judge does not punish a crime against the country. He decides who owes what to whom: pay back, stop, or keep a promise.
decouverte.enVrai: In civil law, a plaintiff sues another private party. He wants money for a loss, or an end to a dispute. The judge says if the defendant is liable (responsible) or not. A liable defendant may have to pay damages, which is money for the harm. The image has limits: a civil court must follow precise laws.

decouverte.question: In a civil trial, can a defendant who is found liable be sent to prison for that?
options: No, civil liability does not lead to prison
Yes, like in a criminal case
decouverte.answer: No, civil liability does not lead to prison
decouverte.explanation: In a civil case, you are liable or not. You may have to pay or to stop an activity. But refusing to obey a court order can lead to jail.

decouverte.titre: Two cases that involve your company
decouverte.texte: Case 1: a stranger steals data from your system. Your company asks for damages in court. You collect the logs that prove the fault. Case 2: a former employee says the company treated him badly. You must keep all the emails. A request to keep evidence is called a litigation hold.
Before a trial, a worker fixes a mistake in an original file. Now nobody can trust the file. The judge may refuse to use it. This is called spoliation: changing or destroying the original evidence.

cards.question: Official definition: “civil law”
cards.answer: Civil law governs relations and interactions between private entities. The plaintiff in a civil case sues for compensation for a loss or relief from some type of dispute.
cards.explanation: In simple words: civil law is about disputes between private parties. One side asks for compensation, which is money for a loss.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Civil”. A private entity is a person or a company, not the State.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “civil law”?
options: Civil law governs relations and interactions between governments and private entities. The plaintiff in a civil case sues for compensation for a loss or relief from some type of dispute.
Civil law governs relations and interactions between private entities. The plaintiff in a civil case sues for imprisonment of the offender or relief from some type of dispute.
Civil law governs relations and interactions between private entities. The plaintiff in a civil case sues for compensation for a loss or relief from some type of dispute.
Civil law governs relations and interactions between private entities. The prosecutor in a civil case sues for compensation for a loss or relief from some type of dispute.
options_why: A civil case is between private parties. The State is not one side of it.
Prison is not a civil result. The plaintiff asks for compensation or relief.
A prosecutor works in criminal cases. In civil cases, the person who sues is the plaintiff.
cards.answer: Civil law governs relations and interactions between private entities. The plaintiff in a civil case sues for compensation for a loss or relief from some type of dispute.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: private entities, the plaintiff, and compensation for a loss.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “civil law” from memory.
cards.answer: Civil law governs relations and interactions between private entities. The plaintiff in a civil case sues for compensation for a loss or relief from some type of dispute.
cards.explanation: Three parts: relations between private entities, the plaintiff who sues, and compensation for a loss.

cards.question: Official definition: the standard of proof of a civil trial
cards.answer: Unlike criminal law, in civil proceedings, the usual standard of proof is preponderance of the evidence, meaning it is a much lower burden of proof.
cards.explanation: In simple words: civil cases use a much lower level of proof than criminal cases.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about the standard of proof of a civil trial from memory.
cards.answer: Unlike criminal law, in civil proceedings, the usual standard of proof is preponderance of the evidence, meaning it is a much lower burden of proof.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the usual standard, its name, and the fact that it is much lower.

cards.question: Official definition: “liable” and “guilty” in a civil trial
cards.answer: In a civil proceeding, there is no question of guilty versus not guilty but rather liable versus not liable.
cards.explanation: In simple words: in a civil case, the court asks if you are liable, not if you are guilty.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about liable and guilty in a civil trial from memory.
cards.answer: In a civil proceeding, there is no question of guilty versus not guilty but rather liable versus not liable.
cards.explanation: Three parts: no question of guilt, versus, and liable or not liable.

cards.question: Official definition: “spoliation of evidence”
cards.answer: Spoliation of evidence (i.e., altering or destruction of the original) can lead to exclusion of evidence in a case or, in some situations, can lead to a separate lawsuit for the damages resulting from the spoliation.
cards.explanation: In simple words: spoliation is changing or destroying the original evidence. The evidence can be thrown out.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Civil”. Exclusion means that the judge does not accept the evidence.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “spoliation of evidence”?
options: Spoliation of evidence (i.e., altering or destruction of the original) can lead to exclusion of evidence in a case or, in some situations, can lead to a separate lawsuit for the damages resulting from the spoliation.

Spoliation of evidence (i.e., copying of the original) can lead to exclusion of evidence in a case or, in some situations, can lead to a separate lawsuit for the damages resulting from the spoliation.

Spoliation of evidence (i.e., altering or destruction of the original) can lead to acceptance of the evidence in a case or, in some situations, can lead to a separate lawsuit for the damages resulting from the spoliation.

Spoliation of evidence (i.e., altering or destruction of the original) can lead to exclusion of evidence in a case or, in some situations, but never to a separate lawsuit for the damages resulting from the spoliation.
options_why: Copying is not spoliation. Spoliation is altering or destroying the original.
Spoliation does the opposite: the evidence can be excluded.
A separate lawsuit is possible in some situations.
cards.answer: Spoliation of evidence (i.e., altering or destruction of the original) can lead to exclusion of evidence in a case or, in some situations, can lead to a separate lawsuit for the damages resulting from the spoliation.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: altering or destruction, exclusion of evidence, and a separate lawsuit.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “spoliation of evidence” from memory.
cards.answer: Spoliation of evidence (i.e., altering or destruction of the original) can lead to exclusion of evidence in a case or, in some situations, can lead to a separate lawsuit for the damages resulting from the spoliation.
cards.explanation: Three parts: altering or destroying the original, evidence excluded, or a separate lawsuit.

cards.question: In a civil case, which question does the court answer?
options: Is the defendant guilty or not guilty?
Did the defendant harm the State?
Did the defendant break an internal rule?
Is the defendant liable or not liable?
options_why: That is the question of a criminal case. Civil cases use liable.
The State is not a party in a civil case.
Internal rules belong to administrative investigations.
cards.answer: Is the defendant liable or not liable?
cards.explanation: In a civil case, there is no question of guilty or not guilty, but of liable or not liable.

cards.question: Who does most of the evidence work in a civil case?
options: Law enforcement officers with badges
IT and security professionals, such as CISSPs
Government agents from the State
Only the judge who hears the case
options_why: Officers work on criminal cases. In civil cases, the parties do the work.
Government agents work in criminal and regulatory cases.
The judge decides the case. The judge does not collect the evidence.
cards.answer: IT and security professionals, such as CISSPs
cards.explanation: In civil cases, the investigation is done by IT and security professionals, not by badged law enforcement.

cards.question: A court finds a defendant liable in a civil case. What can the court order?
options: A prison sentence for being liable
Pay damages, or stop a harmful activity
A fine paid to the police
The loss of his job by court order
options_why: Civil liability does not lead to prison.
Fines to the State come from criminal and regulatory cases.
A court does not fire people. It orders payment, a stop, or a promise to be kept.
cards.answer: Pay damages, or stop a harmful activity
cards.explanation: The court can order damages, an end to a harmful activity, or respect for a contract.

cards.question: How much fault is enough to lose a civil trial?
cards.answer: Even 50.1 percent: a simple majority of fault.
cards.explanation: A civil case is satisfied with more than half.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Civil”. Elsewhere, the manual says at least 51 percent. Remember: a little more than half.

cards.question: Which standard of proof is usual in civil cases?
options: Beyond a reasonable doubt
Whatever management chooses to believe
Proof by a signed confession
Preponderance of the evidence
options_why: That is the higher level for criminal cases.
That is how administrative investigations work.
A confession is not needed in a civil case.
cards.answer: Preponderance of the evidence
cards.explanation: Civil cases use a much lower level of proof than criminal cases.

cards.question: A lawyer tells you that a former employee plans to sue your company. The lawyer asks you to keep all emails. What is the BEST action?
options: Make sure no email is destroyed until told otherwise
Delete the old emails to lower the risk for the company
Fix the emails that could cause confusion in court
Keep only the emails that help the company in court
options_why: Destroying evidence is spoliation. It can get the evidence thrown out.
Changing originals is spoliation. Originals must not be changed.
Choosing only helpful emails hides evidence. All emails must be kept.
cards.answer: Make sure no email is destroyed until told otherwise
cards.explanation: Evidence must be kept when a court or a lawyer asks for it. This is a litigation hold.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a possible result of a civil lawsuit?
options: An order to pay damages
An order to stop a harmful activity
A prison sentence for being liable
An order to keep a contract
options_why: This is a possible result. Damages are money for the harm.
This is a possible result. The court can end a harmful activity.
This is a possible result. The court can order a promise to be kept.
cards.answer: A prison sentence for being liable
cards.explanation: Being liable in a civil case does not lead to prison.

cards.question: What can a court order a liable defendant to do?
cards.answer: Pay damages, stop an activity that harms the plaintiff, or respect a contract.
cards.explanation: These are duties, not prison sentences.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Civil”. Refusing to obey a court order can lead to a charge of contempt of court, and then to jail.

cards.question: Your company is the plaintiff after a data theft. Which evidence is MOST useful to show that the defendant caused the harm?
options: The company's security policy and its staff handbook
A list of all employees
Logs from the attacked computers and the network
The company's yearly financial report
options_why: A policy shows rules, not what the defendant did.
A list of employees does not show who caused the harm.
A financial report may show the loss, but not who caused it.
cards.answer: Logs from the attacked computers and the network
cards.explanation: Logs tell what happened, step by step. They can show that the defendant caused the harm.

cards.question: A judge may refuse evidence that seems unreliable. What is the BEST way to protect the evidence you collect?
options: Keep the originals and document the chain of custody
Edit the originals to make them easier for the judge to read
Delete the extra copies of the files
Give the originals to the other side to check
options_why: Originals must never be altered, with very few exceptions.
Deleting copies does not protect the evidence and may hide facts.
Handing over originals without advice from counsel can put them at risk.
cards.answer: Keep the originals and document the chain of custody
cards.explanation: Keeping the original copies and a clear chain of custody makes the evidence more reliable.

cards.question: What is a litigation hold?
cards.answer: An order to keep possible evidence and to stop it from being destroyed. It is also called a preservation notice.
cards.explanation: It protects the evidence while a case is open.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Civil”: destruction hold notice, preservation notice, litigation hold, or similar terms.

cards.question: Why is the effort to collect evidence lower in civil cases than in criminal cases? Which reason is MOST accurate?
options: Civil evidence does not need to be reliable
Original evidence can be changed freely
Civil cases never reach a judge
The standard of proof and the stakes are lower
options_why: Unreliable evidence may be excluded by the judge.
Originals must not be changed, with very few exceptions.
Civil cases do reach a judge.
cards.answer: The standard of proof and the stakes are lower
cards.explanation: Lower stakes do not mean less care. Due care must still be taken.

cards.question: What can happen if someone destroys original evidence?
options: The evidence becomes stronger
The evidence may be excluded, or a lawsuit may follow
The plaintiff wins the case at once
Nothing, if a copy exists
options_why: Destroying evidence does not make it stronger.
The court does not give a win for this.
A copy does not remove the problem. Destroying originals is spoliation.
cards.answer: The evidence may be excluded, or a lawsuit may follow
cards.explanation: This is spoliation. It can lead to excluded evidence or to a separate lawsuit.

cards.question: A civil litigant refuses to obey a court order. What can happen?
options: Nothing, because civil cases never lead to jail
A charge of contempt of court, which could lead to jail
The case moves to a regulatory agency
The court gives the plaintiff everything he asks for
options_why: Being liable does not lead to jail, but refusing an order can.
Agencies do not take over civil cases.
Refusing an order is not rewarded with a win.
cards.answer: A charge of contempt of court, which could lead to jail
cards.explanation: Contempt of court means disobeying the court. It could eventually lead to jail.

cards.question: Name two kinds of logs you may collect when your company is the plaintiff after a data theft.
cards.answer: Logs from the attacked computers, from intrusion detection systems, and from network devices (any two).
cards.explanation: These logs show what happened, step by step.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Civil”. An intrusion detection system spots suspicious access.

paragraphes: A government inspector visits the school canteen. He checks the fridges, the dates and the cleaning.
Nobody called him to complain. He decides to come by himself.
If he finds a fault, he can give a fine or order the canteen to stop. This kind of check is called a regulatory investigation.

decouverte.titre: The inspector with the power of the law
decouverte.comme: The inspector does not give advice. He applies rules that have the force of law. These rules protect the students.
decouverte.enVrai: A regulation is an official rule: a law made by a public body. It protects citizens or the environment, or makes an industry safer. A regulatory investigation checks that an organization follows the rule. The image has limits: an inspector only has power in his own field.

decouverte.question: PCI DSS is a set of rules for card payments. Shops choose it by contract. Is it a regulation in the sense of the manual?
options: Yes: it is a mandatory law
No: it is a standard set by contract
decouverte.answer: No: it is a standard set by contract
decouverte.explanation: A regulation is a law set by a public body. PCI DSS is a contract standard. Only those who choose it must follow it.

decouverte.texte: In the United States, the EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) is a government agency. It writes regulations about toxic waste and the transport of some products. These regulations have the force of law. Someone who breaks them can be prosecuted by the government.

cards.question: Official definition: “regulatory investigations”
cards.answer: Regulatory investigations involve determining whether an organization is compliant with a given regulation or legal requirement.
cards.explanation: In simple words: an agency checks if an organization follows a law or a rule.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Regulatory”. Compliant means that the organization follows the rule.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “regulatory investigations”?
options: Regulatory investigations involve determining whether an individual is guilty of a given crime or criminal offense.
Regulatory investigations involve determining whether an organization is compliant with a given standard or internal policy.
Regulatory investigations involve proving that an organization is at fault with a given regulation or legal requirement.
Regulatory investigations involve determining whether an organization is compliant with a given regulation or legal requirement.
options_why: This describes a criminal investigation of a person. Regulatory investigations check an organization.
Standards and internal policies are not regulations. A regulation is a law.
Regulators check if the organization is compliant. They do not start by looking for fault.
cards.answer: Regulatory investigations involve determining whether an organization is compliant with a given regulation or legal requirement.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: determining whether, compliant, and regulation or legal requirement.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “regulatory investigations” from memory.
cards.answer: Regulatory investigations involve determining whether an organization is compliant with a given regulation or legal requirement.
cards.explanation: Three parts: determining whether, the organization is compliant, and a given regulation or legal requirement.

cards.question: Official definition: “regulation” according to (ISC)2
cards.answer: A regulation is not a standard, guideline, or suggestion — it is law, established by a government body.
cards.explanation: In simple words: a regulation is a law made by the government. It is not advice.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Regulatory”. This is from a note in the manual.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “regulation” according to (ISC)2?
options: A regulation is not a standard, guideline, or suggestion — it is law, established by a government body.
A regulation is a standard, guideline, or suggestion — it is not law, but advice from a government body.
A regulation is not a standard, guideline, or suggestion — it is law, established by an industry group.
A regulation is not a standard, guideline, or suggestion — it is a contract, signed with a government body.
options_why: A regulation is the opposite: it is law, not advice.
Industry groups do not make regulations. A government body makes them.
A regulation is a law. A contract is a different thing: PCI DSS is an example.
cards.answer: A regulation is not a standard, guideline, or suggestion — it is law, established by a government body.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: not a standard, it is law, and a government body.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “regulation” according to (ISC)2 from memory.
cards.answer: A regulation is not a standard, guideline, or suggestion — it is law, established by a government body.
cards.explanation: Three parts: what it is not, it is law, and a government body made it.

cards.question: Official definition: regulations and criminal investigations
cards.answer: Regulations have the force of law; consequently, regulatory investigations are similar to criminal investigations.
cards.explanation: In simple words: regulations have the force of law. So checking them is a bit like a criminal case.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about regulations and criminal investigations from memory.
cards.answer: Regulations have the force of law; consequently, regulatory investigations are similar to criminal investigations.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the force of law, similar, and criminal investigations.

cards.question: Official definition: proof and penalties in a regulatory investigation
cards.answer: The burden of proof for regulatory investigations is the preponderance of the evidence, and the penalties typically involve fines and injunctions.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the level of proof is the same as in civil cases. Penalties are fines and official orders.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Regulatory”. An injunction is an official order to do something or to stop doing something.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about proof and penalties in a regulatory investigation from memory.
cards.answer: The burden of proof for regulatory investigations is the preponderance of the evidence, and the penalties typically involve fines and injunctions.
cards.explanation: Two parts: the standard of proof, then the usual penalties.

cards.question: Official definition: PCI-DSS is not a regulation
cards.answer: Conversely, the PCI-DSS is not a regulation, as defined by (ISC)2; the PCI-DSS is a contractual standard, affecting only those parties that voluntarily choose to comply with it (i.e., merchants that accept credit card payment).
cards.explanation: In simple words: PCI-DSS is a contract standard. Only shops that choose it must follow it.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Regulatory”. PCI-DSS is a set of rules for card payments.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about PCI-DSS from memory.
cards.answer: Conversely, the PCI-DSS is not a regulation, as defined by (ISC)2; the PCI-DSS is a contractual standard, affecting only those parties that voluntarily choose to comply with it (i.e., merchants that accept credit card payment).
cards.explanation: Three parts: not a regulation, a contractual standard, and followed by choice.

cards.question: What does a regulatory investigation check?
options: If an employee broke an internal policy
If a company owes money to another company
If an organization follows a regulation or legal rule
If a suspect committed a crime
options_why: That is an administrative investigation, inside the organization.
That is a civil case between private parties.
That is a criminal investigation, led by law enforcement.
cards.answer: If an organization follows a regulation or legal rule
cards.explanation: A regulatory investigation checks compliance with a law or a rule.

cards.question: Which of these is a regulation in the sense of (ISC)2?
options: The PCI DSS standard for card payments
A good-practice guide from an industry group
A rule written by the EPA about toxic waste
A company's internal security policy
options_why: PCI DSS is a contractual standard. It is not a law.
A guide from a group is advice. It is not a law.
An internal policy is the company's own rule, not a law.
cards.answer: A rule written by the EPA about toxic waste
cards.explanation: A rule from a government agency has the force of law.

cards.question: Who decides when a regulatory investigation starts?
options: The government agency itself
The company being checked
A private plaintiff
The company's lawyer
options_why: The company being checked does not choose to be checked.
A private plaintiff starts a civil case.
A company lawyer advises the company. The agency decides.
cards.answer: The government agency itself
cards.explanation: Agencies have the authority and discretion to decide when to investigate.

cards.question: Who decides to start a regulatory investigation?
cards.answer: The government agencies themselves. They have their own investigators, prosecutors and courts.
cards.explanation: The agency does not wait to be called.

cards.question: What are typical penalties in a regulatory investigation?
options: Always a prison sentence
Only public apologies
Dismissal of employees
Fines and injunctions
options_why: Prison is possible only if the regulator passes the case to criminal law enforcement.
The manual talks about real penalties: fines and injunctions.
Dismissal is an internal penalty from an administrative case.
cards.answer: Fines and injunctions
cards.explanation: The penalties typically involve fines and injunctions.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Regulatory”. The regulator can also ask criminal law enforcement to step in. Then prison is possible.

cards.question: A colleague says: “PCI DSS is a regulation, so it is the law.” What is the BEST reply?
options: You are right, because it protects the consumers of cards
It is a contractual standard, not a regulation
It is a regulation only in the United States
It is a regulation if the company is large
options_why: Protecting consumers is not the test. A regulation must be a law from a government body.
The manual does not say that. It calls PCI DSS a contractual standard.
The size of the company does not change what the standard is.
cards.answer: It is a contractual standard, not a regulation
cards.explanation: Only shops that choose to accept cards must follow PCI DSS.

cards.question: Which statement about a regulation is NOT correct for (ISC)2?
options: It is established by a government body
It is a suggestion that companies can ignore
It has the force of law
Breaking it can lead to prosecution
options_why: This is correct. A government body establishes regulations.
This is correct. A regulation is a law.
This is correct. The government can prosecute someone who breaks a regulation.
cards.answer: It is a suggestion that companies can ignore
cards.explanation: A regulation is not a suggestion. It is law.

cards.question: What is an injunction?
cards.answer: An official order to do something or to stop doing something.
cards.explanation: It often comes along with a fine.
cards.explanation_more: Simple definition, outside the manual. The manual lists injunctions among the typical penalties.

cards.question: Why is a regulatory investigation similar to a criminal investigation? Which reason is MOST accurate?
options: Both are led by the company's own security team
Both always end in a prison sentence
Both use the lowest standard of proof
Regulations have the force of law
options_why: Neither type is led by the company's own team. Regulators and the police lead them.
Regulatory cases usually end in fines and injunctions.
Criminal cases use the highest standard of proof.
cards.answer: Regulations have the force of law
cards.explanation: A rule that has the force of law is checked a bit like a criminal law.

cards.question: Which statement about regulators is LEAST accurate?
options: They must wait for a complaint first
They can ask organizations for information
They can use data from audit reports
They have their own investigators, prosecutors and courts
options_why: This is accurate. Regulators can demand information.
This is accurate. Audit report data can replace their own work.
This is accurate. Agencies have their own staff and courts.
cards.answer: They must wait for a complaint first
cards.explanation: Agencies decide by themselves when to investigate. They do not wait for a complaint.

cards.question: What can a regulator do instead of running its own investigation?
cards.answer: Ask the organization for information, or use data from audit reports.
cards.explanation: It can rely on what the organization provides.

cards.question: A regulator finds proof of a crime during a regulatory investigation. What can it do?
options: Do nothing, because it can only give fines
Close the case without any action
Ask criminal law enforcement to take over
Give the evidence to the company's competitors
options_why: Regulators can refer the case to criminal law enforcement.
Proof of a crime should not be dropped.
This would be unfair and harmful. Evidence goes to the right authority.
cards.answer: Ask criminal law enforcement to take over
cards.explanation: A regulatory investigation can lead to a criminal one. Prison is then possible.

cards.question: Which standard of proof applies to regulatory investigations?
options: Beyond a reasonable doubt
Whatever the regulator's manager believes
Preponderance of the evidence
No standard of proof at all
options_why: That is the criminal standard.
That describes administrative investigations, which are internal.
Regulators need proof. The standard is preponderance of the evidence.
cards.answer: Preponderance of the evidence
cards.explanation: It is the same standard as in civil cases: more likely than not.

cards.question: Which of these is a typical goal of a regulation?
options: To protect consumers and the environment
To raise the profits of large companies
To replace the internal policies of companies
To help the police find suspects
options_why: Regulations are not made to raise company profits.
Companies still need their own policies.
Regulations protect the public. They are not a tool to find suspects.
cards.answer: To protect consumers and the environment
cards.explanation: Regulations are written to protect citizens or consumers, protect the environment, or make an industry safer.

cards.question: Why is PCI DSS not a regulation for (ISC)2?
cards.answer: It is a contractual standard. Only those who choose to follow it are affected.
cards.explanation: A regulation is a law made by a government body.

paragraphes: In science class, you follow a method. You observe, you take notes, you keep the sample untouched, you analyze, then you write a report.
If you skip a step, nobody believes your result.
For digital evidence (files, phones, logs), organizations have written similar methods. They are standards and guides.

decouverte.comme: The lab protocol says what to do, and in which order, so that the result can be trusted. It is a guide that people follow.
decouverte.enVrai: Investigation standards give steps for handling digital evidence. They also cover security incidents, which are events that threaten security, like a data leak. Digital forensics means using science to find and study this evidence. The image has limits: some standards depend on your country or your industry.

decouverte.question: A standard gives four steps to handle digital evidence. Which order is right?
options: Identify, collect, acquire, preserve
Analyze, erase, copy, report
Copy, analyze, identify, report
decouverte.explanation: First you find what to take. Then you collect it, get a usable copy (acquire), and keep it safe (preserve).

decouverte.texte: An employee is suspected of copying files onto his phone. A phone is not like other computers: its memory and files are organized in a different way. A NIST guide explains how to get, keep, examine and study its evidence, then write a report. A phone is also private, so you must be careful.

cards.question: Official definition: “ISO/IEC 27037:2012”
cards.answer: ISO/IEC 27037:2012 provides guidelines for handling digital evidence. This is covered through a four-step process of identification, collection, acquisition, and preservation.
cards.explanation: In simple words: it is a guide to handle digital evidence in four steps.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Industry Standards”. ISO is the International Organization for Standardization. Digital evidence is evidence kept on computers and phones.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “ISO/IEC 27037:2012”?
options: ISO/IEC 27037:2012 provides guidelines for handling digital evidence. This is covered through a four-step process of identification, collection, examination, and reporting.
ISO/IEC 27037:2012 provides guidelines for handling security incidents. This is covered through a four-step process of identification, collection, acquisition, and preservation.
ISO/IEC 27037:2012 provides guidelines for handling digital evidence. This is covered through a three-step process of identification, collection, and preservation.
ISO/IEC 27037:2012 provides guidelines for handling digital evidence. This is covered through a four-step process of identification, collection, acquisition, and preservation.
options_why: Examination and reporting belong to the phases of NIST SP 800-86.
ISO/IEC 27037 is about digital evidence. Incident investigations are in ISO/IEC 27043.
There are four steps, not three. Acquisition is the missing step.
cards.answer: ISO/IEC 27037:2012 provides guidelines for handling digital evidence. This is covered through a four-step process of identification, collection, acquisition, and preservation.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: digital evidence, and a four-step process.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “ISO/IEC 27037:2012” from memory.
cards.answer: ISO/IEC 27037:2012 provides guidelines for handling digital evidence. This is covered through a four-step process of identification, collection, acquisition, and preservation.
cards.explanation: Four steps in order: identification, collection, acquisition, preservation.

cards.question: Official definition: “NIST SP 800-86”
cards.answer: Most importantly, NIST SP 800-86 describes the digital forensic process overall in four phases: collection, examination, analysis, and reporting.
cards.explanation: In simple words: the digital forensic process has four phases. You collect, examine, analyze and report.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Industry Standards”. Its title is “Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response”.

cards.question: Which sentence is the official definition of “NIST SP 800-86”?
options: Most importantly, NIST SP 800-86 describes the digital forensic process overall in four phases: identification, collection, acquisition, and preservation.
Most importantly, NIST SP 800-86 describes the digital forensic process overall in four phases: collection, examination, analysis, and reporting.
Most importantly, NIST SP 800-86 describes the digital forensic process overall in three phases: collection, analysis, and reporting.
Most importantly, NIST SP 800-86 describes the digital forensic process overall in four phases: preparation, collection, analysis, and reporting.
options_why: These four steps come from ISO/IEC 27037, not from NIST SP 800-86.
There are four phases. Examination is the missing phase.
Preparation is not one of the four phases. The second phase is examination.
cards.answer: Most importantly, NIST SP 800-86 describes the digital forensic process overall in four phases: collection, examination, analysis, and reporting.
cards.explanation: Look at the key words: digital forensic process, and four phases.

cards.question: Say the official definition of “NIST SP 800-86” from memory.
cards.answer: Most importantly, NIST SP 800-86 describes the digital forensic process overall in four phases: collection, examination, analysis, and reporting.
cards.explanation: Four phases in order: collection, examination, analysis, reporting.

cards.question: Official definition: “ISO/IEC 27043:2015”
cards.answer: ISO/IEC 27043:2015 recommends procedural steps for conducting security incident investigations.
cards.explanation: In simple words: it gives the steps to investigate a security incident.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Industry Standards”. A security incident is an event that threatens security, like a data leak.

cards.question: Say the official sentence about “ISO/IEC 27043:2015” from memory.
cards.answer: ISO/IEC 27043:2015 recommends procedural steps for conducting security incident investigations.
cards.explanation: Two parts: procedural steps, and security incident investigations.

cards.question: Official definition: “NIST SP 800-101 Revision 1”
cards.answer: NIST SP 800-101 Revision 1, "Guidelines on Mobile Device Forensics," has a self-explanatory title. It covers the unique requirements for acquiring, preserving, examining, analyzing, and reporting on the digital evidence present on mobile devices.
cards.explanation: In simple words: it is the guide for evidence on phones and tablets.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Industry Standards”. A mobile device is, for example, a phone or a tablet.

cards.question: Say the official text about “NIST SP 800-101 Revision 1” from memory.
cards.answer: NIST SP 800-101 Revision 1, "Guidelines on Mobile Device Forensics," has a self-explanatory title. It covers the unique requirements for acquiring, preserving, examining, analyzing, and reporting on the digital evidence present on mobile devices.
cards.explanation: Three parts: the title, the unique requirements, and the five actions on the evidence.

cards.question: Which publication has four steps: identification, collection, acquisition and preservation?
options: NIST SP 800-86
ISO/IEC 27037
NIST SP 800-101
ISO/IEC 27043
options_why: NIST SP 800-86 has four different phases: collection, examination, analysis and reporting.
NIST SP 800-101 is the guide for mobile devices.
ISO/IEC 27043 gives steps for investigating security incidents.
cards.answer: ISO/IEC 27037
cards.explanation: ISO/IEC 27037 is the guide for handling digital evidence in four steps.

cards.question: Which publication describes four phases: collection, examination, analysis and reporting?
options: ISO/IEC 27037
NIST SP 800-101
ISO/IEC 27043
NIST SP 800-86
options_why: ISO/IEC 27037 has four different steps: identification, collection, acquisition and preservation.
NIST SP 800-101 is the guide for mobile devices.
ISO/IEC 27043 gives steps for investigating security incidents.
cards.answer: NIST SP 800-86
cards.explanation: NIST SP 800-86 describes the digital forensic process in four phases.

cards.question: You must examine the phone of a suspected employee. Which publication is made for this?
options: NIST SP 800-101
NIST SP 800-86
ISO/IEC 27043
ISO/IEC 27037
options_why: NIST SP 800-86 is the general guide to digital forensics, not the one for phones.
ISO/IEC 27043 gives steps for investigating security incidents, not for phones.
ISO/IEC 27037 covers many media, but the NIST guide is made for mobile devices.
cards.answer: NIST SP 800-101
cards.explanation: NIST SP 800-101 covers the unique needs of mobile devices.

cards.question: In which years were ISO/IEC 27043 and ISO/IEC 27037 published?
cards.explanation: The lower number, 27037, is the older one.

cards.question: What does ISO/IEC 27043 give?
options: Rules for building a forensic team
A list of court orders by country
Steps for investigating security incidents
Tools to copy mobile phones
options_why: Building a forensic capability is in NIST SP 800-86.
Court orders depend on the country. This standard does not list them.
Phones are covered by NIST SP 800-101.
cards.answer: Steps for investigating security incidents
cards.explanation: It recommends procedural steps from preparation to the end of the investigation.

cards.question: In ISO/IEC 27037, which step comes right AFTER collection?
options: Identification
Preservation
Acquisition
Reporting
options_why: Identification comes first, before collection.
Preservation comes last, after acquisition.
Reporting is a phase of NIST SP 800-86, not a step of ISO/IEC 27037.
cards.answer: Acquisition
cards.explanation: The order is identification, collection, acquisition, then preservation.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT a phase of NIST SP 800-86?
options: Acquisition of the evidence
Collection of the evidence
Examination of the digital evidence
Reporting of the results
options_why: This is a phase of NIST SP 800-86.
This is a phase of NIST SP 800-86.
This is a phase of NIST SP 800-86.
cards.answer: Acquisition of the evidence
cards.explanation: Acquisition is a step of ISO/IEC 27037. The NIST phases are collection, examination, analysis and reporting.

cards.question: What is the title of NIST SP 800-86?
cards.answer: “Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response”.
cards.explanation: It adds forensic techniques to incident response.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Industry Standards”. It also describes the tools and training that your staff needs.

cards.question: Your company wants to build a digital forensic capability. Which publication is BEST to read?
options: NIST SP 800-101
ISO/IEC 27043
ISO/IEC 27037
NIST SP 800-86
options_why: NIST SP 800-101 is about mobile devices only.
ISO/IEC 27043 gives steps for investigating incidents.
ISO/IEC 27037 is about handling the evidence, not about building the capability.
cards.answer: NIST SP 800-86
cards.explanation: NIST SP 800-86 explains how to build this capability, with the tools, the training and the policies.

cards.question: Which statement about ISO/IEC 27037 is MOST accurate?
options: It covers only paper evidence
It covers digital evidence and the chain of custody
It is only about mobile phones
It replaces the law of each country
options_why: It is about digital evidence on many media.
Phones are one type among many media.
A standard does not replace laws.
cards.answer: It covers digital evidence and the chain of custody
cards.explanation: It also covers how to exchange evidence between jurisdictions.

cards.question: What does ISO/IEC 27037 cover besides the four steps?
cards.answer: The chain of custody and the exchange of evidence between jurisdictions.
cards.explanation: It also covers many kinds of media: disks, mobiles, cameras, computers and network data.

cards.question: A manager says: “Phones work like computers, so any guide will do.” What is the BEST reply?
options: You are right, the same steps always fit
Phones differ, so use the mobile device guide
Phones cannot be used as evidence
Only the police can look at phones
options_why: Memory and file structure differ on phones.
Phones can hold important digital evidence.
A company can look at its own devices, with care.
cards.answer: Phones differ, so use the mobile device guide
cards.explanation: NIST SP 800-101 covers the unique needs of mobile devices.

cards.question: Which incidents does ISO/IEC 27043 cover?
options: Only thefts of equipment
Only fires and floods
Only tax fraud
Data loss, unauthorized access and data breaches
options_why: Equipment theft is not the only case.
Fires and floods are not security incidents of this kind.
Tax fraud is a different field.
cards.answer: Data loss, unauthorized access and data breaches
cards.explanation: It covers data loss, corruption, unauthorized access and confirmed data breaches.

cards.question: What does NIST SP 800-101 cover?
cards.answer: Digital evidence on mobile devices: phones and tablets.
cards.explanation: Their memory and file structure are different from computers.

cards.question: Why follow a recognized standard when you handle digital evidence?
options: So that the evidence stays reliable
So that the evidence can be changed safely
So that the police can skip their own rules
So that management does not need to be told
options_why: Evidence must not be changed.
The police still follow their own rules.
Management still needs to know.
cards.answer: So that the evidence stays reliable
cards.explanation: A recognized method shows that every step was done with care.

cards.question: Why do phones need their own forensic guide?
cards.answer: Their memory and file structure are different. They are also often private.
cards.explanation: A careful guide helps you protect both the evidence and the owner.
